items.stem: What is meant by one radian?
options: The angle subtended by an arc equal in length to the diameter
The angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius
The angle swept out in one second
items.answer: The angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius
items.markingKey: θ = s/r; θ = 1 rad when s = r.

items.stem: Use the definition of the radian to show that v = ωr for an object moving in a circle at constant speed.
items.answer: Arc length s = rθ; dividing by time t gives s/t = r(θ/t), i.e. v = ωr.
items.markingKey: s = rθ from definition of radian [1]; divide by t to give v = ωr [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why an object moving in a circle at constant speed is accelerating.
items.answer: Its direction of motion changes continuously, so its velocity changes; acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
items.markingKey: velocity is a vector / direction changes [1]; acceleration = rate of change of velocity [1] [2]

items.stem: During a visit to a science centre, Lina notes that a vinyl record of radius 0.13 m rotates at 33 revolutions per minute. Calculate the angular speed.
items.answer: 3.46 rad s⁻¹
items.markingKey: ω = 2π × 33/60 = 3.46 rad s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: During a visit to a science centre, Kenji notes that a London-Eye style observation wheel of radius 68.2 m completes one revolution every 2100 s. Calculate the angular speed and the linear speed of a point on the rim.
A washing-machine drum of radius 0.23 m rotates at 1000 revolutions per minute. (a) Define the radian. (b) Calculate the linear speed of a point on the rim.
items.answer: (a) The angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius. (b) 24.1 m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) arc length = radius [1]; angle at centre [1] [2] (b) v = ωr (method/substitution) [1]; answer 24.1 m s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: How many radians are there in one complete revolution?
items.answer: 2π rad

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What is the angular speed of the minute hand of a clock? (b) What is the SI unit of angular speed?
items.answer: (a) 1.75 × 10⁻³ rad s⁻¹ (b) rad s⁻¹

items.stem: Explain why a point on the Earth's equator has a greater linear speed than a point at latitude 60° N, although both have the same angular speed.
items.answer: Both turn through 2π rad in one day, so ω is the same; the point at 60° N moves in a circle of smaller radius (R cos 60°), and v = ωr.
items.markingKey: same ω (same period) [1]; smaller radius of circle at 60° so smaller v = ωr [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the radian is described as having no dimensions.
items.answer: It is defined as a ratio of two lengths (arc length ÷ radius), so the units cancel.
items.markingKey: ratio of arc length to radius [1]; units of length cancel [1] [2]

items.stem: A student says that the hour hand of a clock has a greater angular speed than the minute hand because it is shorter. Explain why the student is wrong.
items.answer: Angular speed depends only on the time for one revolution: the hour hand takes 12 h, the minute hand 1 h, so the minute hand has the greater ω; length affects only the linear speed of the tip.
items.markingKey: ω = 2π/T, independent of length [1]; minute hand has shorter T so larger ω [1] [2]

items.stem: Compare the angular speeds of the hour hand of a clock and the Earth orbiting the Sun. Explain which is greater and calculate the ratio of the larger to the smaller.
items.answer: ω = 2π/T; the hour hand of a clock has the shorter period so the greater ω; ratio = 731
items.markingKey: ω = 2π/T, so ω ∝ 1/T [1]; correct identification of larger ω [1]; ratio = T_long/T_short = 731 [1] [3]

items.stem: A data sheet states that a car wheel of radius 0.29 m rotates at 600 revolutions per minute. What is the angular speed?
items.answer: 62.8 rad s⁻¹

items.stem: A point on a rotating door moves through an angle of 300° on a circular path of radius 0.45 m. Work out the distance moved along the arc.
items.markingKey: θ = 300 × π/180 = 5.24 rad; s = rθ = 0.45 × 5.24 = 2.36 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: In Kathmandu, a wind-turbine blade of length 52.2 m rotates at 15 revolutions per minute. Determine the angular speed.
items.answer: 1.57 rad s⁻¹
items.markingKey: ω = 2π × 15/60 = 1.57 rad s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A runner on a curved bend moves through an angle of 135° on a circular path of radius 0.80 m. The movement takes 2.4 s at constant speed. Calculate the angular displacement in radians and the angular speed.
items.answer: θ = 2.36 rad; ω = 0.982 rad s⁻¹

items.stem: A vinyl record of radius 0.16 m rotates at 45 revolutions per minute. Calculate the angular speed and the linear speed of a point on the rim.
items.answer: ω = 4.71 rad s⁻¹; v = 0.754 m s⁻¹

items.stem: A vinyl record of radius 0.13 m rotates at 45 revolutions per minute. (a) Calculate the angular speed. (b) Calculate the linear speed of a point on the rim.
items.answer: (a) 4.71 rad s⁻¹ (b) 0.613 m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) ω = 2π/T or 2πf (method/substitution) [1]; answer 4.71 rad s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (b) v = ωr (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.613 m s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: A London-Eye style observation wheel of radius 62.1 m completes one revolution every 1200 s. (a) Calculate the angular speed. (b) Calculate the linear speed of a point halfway between the axis and the rim. (c) Explain why a point on the rim is accelerating even though its speed is constant. (d) Calculate the time for the rim to turn through 3π/2 rad.
items.answer: (a) 0.00524 rad s⁻¹ (b) 0.163 m s⁻¹ (c) Its direction changes continuously so its velocity changes. (d) 900 s
items.markingKey: (a) ω = 2π/T or 2πf (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.00524 rad s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (b) same ω, half radius: 0.163 m s⁻¹ [1] (c) Its direction changes continuously so its velocity changes [1] (d) t = θ/ω (method/substitution) [1]; answer 900 s with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: An object moves in a circle at constant speed. In which direction is its acceleration?
options: along the tangent opposite to the motion
along the tangent in the direction of motion
towards the centre of the circle
items.answer: towards the centre of the circle
items.markingKey: Centripetal acceleration is directed towards the centre.

items.stem: Explain why the centripetal force does not change the speed of an object moving in a circle.
items.answer: The force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it has no component along the direction of motion; no work is done and the kinetic energy (speed) stays constant, only the direction changes.
items.markingKey: force perpendicular to velocity [1]; no work done / KE constant, only direction changes [1] [2]

items.stem: A passenger in a car turning a corner feels pushed outwards. Explain, using Newton's first law, what is actually happening.
items.answer: The passenger tends to continue in a straight line (inertia); the car turns beneath them, so the door pushes inwards on them to provide the centripetal force; there is no outward force on them.
items.markingKey: tendency to continue in straight line [1]; door/seat provides inward force, no outward force [1] [2]

items.stem: A train of mass 2.00 × 10⁵ kg moves round a curve of radius 400 m at a constant speed of 20 m s⁻¹. Determine the centripetal force.
items.markingKey: F = mv²/r = 2.00 × 10⁵ × 20²/400 = 2.00 × 10⁵ N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A car of mass 1500 kg moves round a bend of radius 25 m at a constant speed of 20 m s⁻¹. Calculate the angular speed and the centripetal force, and state what provides this force.
items.answer: ω = 0.80 rad s⁻¹; F = 24 000 N; provided by friction between the tyres and the road
items.markingKey: ω = v/r = 0.80 rad s⁻¹ [1]; F = mv²/r = 24 000 N [1]; friction between the tyres and the road [1] [3]

items.stem: An aircraft of mass 80 000 kg moves round a horizontal circle of radius 2000 m at a constant speed of 240 m s⁻¹. (a) Calculate the centripetal force. (b) The maximum force that the horizontal component of the lift force can provide is 3.46 × 10⁶ N. Calculate the maximum speed for this radius. (c) Explain what happens if this speed is exceeded.
items.answer: (a) 2.30 × 10⁶ N (b) 294 m s⁻¹ (c) the force available is less than mv²/r, so the path curves less sharply: it moves outwards to a larger radius (skids)
items.markingKey: (a) F = mv²/r = 2.30 × 10⁶ N [1] (b) v = √(Fr/m) [1]; = 294 m s⁻¹ [1] (c) insufficient centripetal force [1]; moves to larger radius / skids outwards [1] [5]

items.stem: A ball of mass 0.050 kg on a string moves at constant speed 4.5 m s⁻¹ round a horizontal circle of radius 0.40 m on a smooth table. (a) Explain why a resultant force is needed even though the speed is constant. (b) Calculate the centripetal force.
items.answer: (a) The direction of the velocity changes, so there is an acceleration (towards the centre), which requires a resultant force (F = ma). (b) 2.53 N
items.markingKey: (a) velocity changes [1]; resultant force towards centre [1] [2] (b) F = mv²/r (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.53 N with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: A runner of mass 55 kg moves at constant speed 8.0 m s⁻¹ round a bend of radius 40 m. (a) Explain why a resultant force is needed even though the speed is constant. (b) Calculate the centripetal force. (c) State what provides the centripetal force.
items.answer: (a) The direction of the velocity changes, so there is an acceleration (towards the centre), which requires a resultant force (F = ma). (b) 88 N (c) Friction between the shoes and the track.
items.markingKey: (a) velocity changes [1]; resultant force towards centre [1] [2] (b) F = mv²/r (method/substitution) [1]; answer 88 N with unit [1] [2] (c) Friction between the shoes and the track [1]

items.stem: Which expression gives the centripetal acceleration of an object moving at speed v in a circle of radius r with angular speed ω?
items.answer: rω²
items.markingKey: a = v²/r = rω².

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which expression gives the centripetal acceleration of an object moving at speed v in a circle of radius r with angular speed ω? (b) What provides the centripetal force on the Moon as it orbits the Earth?
items.answer: (a) rω² (b) the gravitational pull of the Earth
items.markingKey: (a) a = v²/r = rω². (b) Gravity acts towards the Earth's centre.

items.stem: A stone is whirled in a horizontal circle on a string and the string breaks. Describe and explain the subsequent motion of the stone (ignore gravity).
items.answer: With no resultant force it moves in a straight line at constant speed along the tangent to the circle at the point of release (Newton's first law).
items.markingKey: tangent to circle [1]; no resultant force so constant velocity [1] [2]

items.stem: Show that the expressions a = v²/r and a = rω² are equivalent.
items.answer: v = ωr, so v²/r = ω²r²/r = rω².
items.markingKey: substitute v = ωr [1]; simplify to rω² [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why centripetal force should not be drawn as an extra force on a free-body diagram.
items.answer: It is not a separate force: it is the name for the resultant of the real forces (tension, friction, gravity, normal force) acting towards the centre.
items.markingKey: centripetal force is a resultant [1]; provided by real forces such as tension or friction [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a car is more likely to skid outwards on a bend when it is travelling fast.
items.answer: The centripetal force needed, mv²/r, increases with v²; friction has a maximum value, so above a certain speed friction cannot supply enough force and the car moves to a larger radius.
items.markingKey: required force ∝ v² [1]; friction limited, so insufficient [1] [2]

items.stem: An aircraft performs a horizontal circular turn. The speed is multiplied by 4 while the mass and radius stay the same. Explain how the centripetal force required changes.
items.answer: The centripetal force required becomes 16 times bigger.
items.markingKey: Using F = mv²/r: centripetal force required ∝ speed^2.00; factor = 4.00^2.00 = 16.0. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why centripetal force should not be drawn as an extra force on a free-body diagram. (b) A stone is whirled in a horizontal circle on a string and the string breaks. Describe and explain the subsequent motion of the stone (ignore gravity).
items.answer: (a) It is not a separate force: it is the name for the resultant of the real forces (tension, friction, gravity, normal force) acting towards the centre. (b) With no resultant force it moves in a straight line at constant speed along the tangent to the circle at the point of release (Newton's first law).
items.markingKey: (a) centripetal force is a resultant [1]; provided by real forces such as tension or friction [1] [2] (b) tangent to circle [1]; no resultant force so constant velocity [1] [2]

items.stem: A cyclist and bicycle of total mass 65 kg moves round a flat bend of radius 18 m at a constant speed of 11 m s⁻¹. What is the centripetal force?
A centrifuge of radius 0.10 m rotates at 4000 revolutions per minute. Calculate the centripetal acceleration at the rim and express it as a multiple of g.
An aircraft of mass 1.20 × 10⁵ kg moves round a horizontal circle of radius 2000 m at a constant speed of 150 m s⁻¹. Determine the centripetal force.
items.markingKey: F = mv²/r = 1.20 × 10⁵ × 150²/2000 = 1.35 × 10⁶ N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A runner of mass 78 kg moves round a bend of radius 45 m at a constant speed of 6.5 m s⁻¹. Determine the centripetal force.
items.markingKey: F = mv²/r = 78 × 6.5²/45 = 73.2 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A astronaut-training centrifuge of radius 9.0 m rotates at 30 revolutions per minute. Calculate the centripetal acceleration at the rim and express it as a multiple of g.
A salad spinner of radius 0.12 m rotates at 240 revolutions per minute. Calculate the centripetal acceleration at the rim and express it as a multiple of g.

A cyclist and bicycle of total mass 65 kg moves round a flat bend of radius 12 m at a constant speed of 9.0 m s⁻¹. Calculate the angular speed and the centripetal force, and state what provides this force.
items.answer: ω = 0.75 rad s⁻¹; F = 439 N; provided by friction between the tyres and the track
items.markingKey: ω = v/r = 0.75 rad s⁻¹ [1]; F = mv²/r = 439 N [1]; friction between the tyres and the track [1] [3]

items.stem: A washing-machine drum of radius 0.25 m rotates at 1200 revolutions per minute. (a) Calculate the centripetal acceleration at the rim. (b) Calculate the resultant force needed to keep an object of mass 0.050 kg at the rim moving in the circle. (c) The rotation rate is doubled. State the factor by which this force changes.

An aircraft of mass 80 000 kg moves at constant speed 120 m s⁻¹ round a horizontal circle of radius 2000 m. (a) Calculate the angular speed. (b) Calculate the centripetal acceleration. (c) State what provides the centripetal force.
items.answer: (a) 0.060 rad s⁻¹ (b) 7.2 m s⁻² (c) The horizontal component of the lift force.
items.markingKey: (a) ω = v/r: 0.060 rad s⁻¹ [1] (b) a = v²/r (method/substitution) [1]; answer 7.2 m s⁻² with unit [1] [2] (c) The horizontal component of the lift force [1]

items.stem: A car of mass 800 kg moves at constant speed 12 m s⁻¹ round a bend of radius 60 m. (a) Explain why a resultant force is needed even though the speed is constant. (b) The speed increases by 50% on the same path. Calculate the new centripetal force.
items.answer: (a) The direction of the velocity changes, so there is an acceleration (towards the centre), which requires a resultant force (F = ma). (b) 4320 N
items.markingKey: (a) velocity changes [1]; resultant force towards centre [1] [2] (b) F ∝ v², × 2.25 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 4320 N with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: A train of mass 2.00 × 10⁵ kg moves at constant speed 20 m s⁻¹ round a curve of radius 900 m. (a) Explain why a resultant force is needed even though the speed is constant. (b) Calculate the centripetal force. (c) The speed increases by 50% on the same path. Calculate the new centripetal force.
items.answer: (a) The direction of the velocity changes, so there is an acceleration (towards the centre), which requires a resultant force (F = ma). (b) 88 900 N (c) 2.00 × 10⁵ N
items.markingKey: (a) velocity changes [1]; resultant force towards centre [1] [2] (b) F = mv²/r (method/substitution) [1]; answer 88 900 N with unit [1] [2] (c) F ∝ v², × 2.25 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.00 × 10⁵ N [1] [2]

items.stem: A car travels round a frictionless banked track at the design speed v. The bank angle is θ and the radius r. Which equation applies?
items.answer: tan θ = v²/(rg)
items.markingKey: N sin θ = mv²/r and N cos θ = mg; divide.

items.stem: A ball on a string moves in a vertical circle. Where is the tension in the string greatest?
options: at the bottom of the circle
at the top of the circle
items.answer: at the bottom of the circle
items.markingKey: T − mg = mv²/r at the bottom: T = mg + mv²/r, and v is also greatest there.

items.stem: Explain how a banked track allows a car to go round a bend without relying on friction.
items.answer: The normal contact force is perpendicular to the tilted surface, so it has a horizontal component towards the centre; at the design speed this component alone provides mv²/r while the vertical component balances the weight.
items.markingKey: normal force tilted [1]; horizontal component provides centripetal force [1] [2]

items.stem: A motorway slip road near Madrid has a bend of radius 200 m. It is banked so that a vehicle travelling at 30 m s⁻¹ needs no sideways friction. Calculate the angle of banking.
items.markingKey: tan θ = v²/(rg) = 30²/(200 × 9.81) = 24.6°. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A roller-coaster car of mass 500 kg is released from rest at a height of 35 m above the bottom of a vertical circular loop of radius 10 m. Friction is negligible. (a) Calculate the minimum speed needed at the top of the loop for the car to stay on the track. (b) Explain why passengers feel heavier at the bottom of the loop.
items.answer: (a) 9.90 m s⁻¹ (b) The seat must push up with N = mg + mv²/r, which is greater than their weight.
items.markingKey: (a) v = √(gr) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 9.90 m s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (b) The seat must push up with N = mg + mv²/r, which is greater than their weight [1]

items.stem: A roller-coaster car just completes a vertical loop of radius r. What is its speed at the top of the loop?
items.answer: √(gr)
items.markingKey: At minimum speed the weight alone provides the centripetal force: mg = mv²/r.

items.stem: Explain why water stays in a bucket swung quickly in a vertical circle, even when the bucket is upside down at the top.
items.answer: At the top, the centripetal force needed (mv²/r) is greater than the weight of the water, so the bucket base must push down on the water; the water stays pressed against the base. If v were too small, mg > mv²/r and the water would fall out.
items.markingKey: required centripetal force > weight [1]; base pushes on water / water stays in contact [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the reading on a scale under a passenger in a big wheel is smaller at the top of the ride than at the bottom.
items.answer: At the top, mg − N = mv²/r, so N = mg − mv²/r < mg; at the bottom, N − mg = mv²/r, so N = mg + mv²/r > mg.
items.markingKey: top: N = mg − mv²/r [1]; bottom: N = mg + mv²/r [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the string of a conical pendulum can never be horizontal.
items.answer: The vertical component of the tension must balance the weight; a horizontal string has no vertical component, so θ < 90° for any finite tension.
items.markingKey: vertical component must equal mg [1]; horizontal string gives zero vertical component [1] [2]

items.stem: A ball of mass 0.50 kg is whirled in a vertical circle of radius 1.2 m on a string. At the top of the circle its speed is 6.0 m s⁻¹. Determine the tension in the string at the top.
items.markingKey: T + mg = mv²/r ⇒ T = 0.50 × 6.0²/1.2 − 0.50 × 9.81 = 10.1 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A model aircraft of mass 0.35 kg is whirled in a vertical circle of radius 1.0 m on a string. At the top of the circle its speed is 7.0 m s⁻¹. Calculate the tension in the string at the top, and the minimum speed at the top for the string to stay taut.
items.answer: T = 13.7 N; v_min = 3.13 m s⁻¹

items.stem: A roller-coaster car of mass 600 kg is released from rest at a height of 30 m above the bottom of a vertical circular loop of radius 10 m. Friction is negligible. (a) Calculate the speed of the car at the top of the loop. (b) Explain why passengers feel heavier at the bottom of the loop.
items.answer: (a) 14.0 m s⁻¹ (b) The seat must push up with N = mg + mv²/r, which is greater than their weight.
items.markingKey: (a) mg(h − 2r) = ½mv² (method/substitution) [1]; answer 14.0 m s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (b) The seat must push up with N = mg + mv²/r, which is greater than their weight [1]

items.stem: A roller-coaster car of mass 500 kg is released from rest at a height of 40 m above the bottom of a vertical circular loop of radius 8.0 m. Friction is negligible. items.stem: A cyclist and bicycle of total mass 65 kg moves round a flat bend of radius 30 m at a constant speed of 9.0 m s⁻¹. Calculate the centripetal force.
items.markingKey: F = mv²/r = 65 × 9.0²/30 = 176 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A centrifuge of radius 0.15 m rotates at 6000 revolutions per minute. Calculate the centripetal acceleration at the rim and express it as a multiple of g.
A salad spinner of radius 0.12 m rotates at 180 revolutions per minute. Calculate the centripetal acceleration at the rim and express it as a multiple of g.

A cyclist and bicycle of total mass 65 kg moves at constant speed 11 m s⁻¹ round a flat bend of radius 25 m. (a) Calculate the angular speed. (b) Calculate the centripetal force. (c) State what provides the centripetal force.
items.answer: (a) 0.44 rad s⁻¹ (b) 315 N (c) Friction between the tyres and the track.
items.markingKey: (a) ω = v/r: 0.44 rad s⁻¹ [1] (b) F = mv²/r (method/substitution) [1]; answer 315 N with unit [1] [2] (c) Friction between the tyres and the track [1]

items.stem: A train of mass 3.50 × 10⁵ kg moves at constant speed 40 m s⁻¹ round a curve of radius 600 m. (a) Explain why a resultant force is needed even though the speed is constant. (b) State what provides the centripetal force. (c) The speed increases by 50% on the same path. Calculate the new centripetal force.
items.answer: (a) The direction of the velocity changes, so there is an acceleration (towards the centre), which requires a resultant force (F = ma). (b) The sideways force of the rails on the wheel flanges. (c) 2.10 × 10⁶ N
items.markingKey: (a) velocity changes [1]; resultant force towards centre [1] [2] (b) The sideways force of the rails on the wheel flanges [1] (c) F ∝ v², × 2.25 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.10 × 10⁶ N [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A car travels round a frictionless banked track at the design speed v. The bank angle is θ and the radius r. Which equation applies? (b) Why does an aircraft bank (tilt its wings) to turn in a horizontal circle?
items.answer: (a) tan θ = v²/(rg) (b) so that a horizontal component of the lift provides the centripetal force
items.markingKey: (a) N sin θ = mv²/r and N cos θ = mg; divide. (b) Lift is perpendicular to the wings; tilting gives it a horizontal component.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why the string of a conical pendulum can never be horizontal. (b) Explain how a banked track allows a car to go round a bend without relying on friction.
items.answer: (a) The vertical component of the tension must balance the weight; a horizontal string has no vertical component, so θ < 90° for any finite tension. (b) The normal contact force is perpendicular to the tilted surface, so it has a horizontal component towards the centre; at the design speed this component alone provides mv²/r while the vertical component balances the weight.
items.markingKey: (a) vertical component must equal mg [1]; horizontal string gives zero vertical component [1] [2] (b) normal force tilted [1]; horizontal component provides centripetal force [1] [2]

items.stem: A conical pendulum consists of a bob of mass 0.20 kg on a string of length 0.40 m. The bob moves in a horizontal circle with the string at 40° to the vertical. Calculate the tension in the string and the radius of the circle.

A conical pendulum consists of a bob of mass 0.15 kg on a string of length 1.0 m. The bob moves in a horizontal circle with the string at 50° to the vertical. Calculate the tension in the string and the radius of the circle.

A roller-coaster car of mass 500 kg is released from rest at a height of 30 m above the bottom of a vertical circular loop of radius 8.0 m. Friction is negligible. (a) Calculate the speed of the car at the top of the loop. (b) Calculate the normal contact force at the bottom of the loop. (c) Explain why passengers feel heavier at the bottom of the loop.
items.answer: (a) 16.6 m s⁻¹ (b) 41 700 N (c) The seat must push up with N = mg + mv²/r, which is greater than their weight.
items.markingKey: (a) mg(h − 2r) = ½mv² (method/substitution) [1]; answer 16.6 m s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (b) N − mg = mv²/r with v² = 2gh (equation) [1]; substitution [1]; answer 41 700 N with unit [1] [3] (c) The seat must push up with N = mg + mv²/r, which is greater than their weight [1]

items.stem: What is the angular speed of the minute hand of a clock?
items.answer: 1.75 × 10⁻³ rad s⁻¹

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A student says that the hour hand of a clock has a greater angular speed than the minute hand because it is shorter. Explain why the student is wrong. (b) Explain why a point on the Earth's equator has a greater linear speed than a point at latitude 60° N, although both have the same angular speed.
items.answer: (a) Angular speed depends only on the time for one revolution: the hour hand takes 12 h, the minute hand 1 h, so the minute hand has the greater ω; length affects only the linear speed of the tip. (b) Both turn through 2π rad in one day, so ω is the same; the point at 60° N moves in a circle of smaller radius (R cos 60°), and v = ωr.
items.markingKey: (a) ω = 2π/T, independent of length [1]; minute hand has shorter T so larger ω [1] [2] (b) same ω (same period) [1]; smaller radius of circle at 60° so smaller v = ωr [1] [2]

items.stem: Compare the angular speeds of the Earth spinning on its axis and the second hand of a clock. Explain which is greater and calculate the ratio of the larger to the smaller.
items.answer: ω = 2π/T; the second hand of a clock has the shorter period so the greater ω; ratio = 1440
items.markingKey: ω = 2π/T, so ω ∝ 1/T [1]; correct identification of larger ω [1]; ratio = T_long/T_short = 1440 [1] [3]

items.stem: A toy train on a circular track moves through an angle of 210° on a circular path of radius 1.2 m. Determine the distance moved along the arc.
items.markingKey: θ = 210 × π/180 = 3.67 rad; s = rθ = 1.2 × 3.67 = 4.40 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: In Seoul, a London-Eye style observation wheel of radius 63.1 m completes one revolution every 1200 s. Determine the angular speed.
items.markingKey: ω = 2π/1200 = 0.00524 rad s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A wind-turbine blade of length 51 m rotates at 18 revolutions per minute. (a) Calculate the linear speed of a point on the rim. (b) Calculate the time for the rim to turn through 3π/2 rad.
items.markingKey: (a) v = ωr (method/substitution) [1]; answer 96.1 m s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (b) t = θ/ω (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.5 s with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: What provides the centripetal force on a car turning a corner on a flat road?
options: friction between the tyres and the road
the driving force of the engine
items.answer: friction between the tyres and the road
items.markingKey: Sideways friction acts towards the centre of the bend.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the centripetal force does not change the speed of an object moving in a circle. (b) Explain why a car is more likely to skid outwards on a bend when it is travelling fast.
items.answer: (a) The force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it has no component along the direction of motion; no work is done and the kinetic energy (speed) stays constant, only the direction changes. (b) The centripetal force needed, mv²/r, increases with v²; friction has a maximum value, so above a certain speed friction cannot supply enough force and the car moves to a larger radius.
items.markingKey: (a) force perpendicular to velocity [1]; no work done / KE constant, only direction changes [1] [2] (b) required force ∝ v² [1]; friction limited, so insufficient [1] [2]

items.stem: An aircraft performs a horizontal circular turn. The radius is multiplied by 5 while the speed and mass stay the same. Explain how the centripetal force required changes.
items.answer: The centripetal force required falls to one fifth.
items.markingKey: Using F = mv²/r: centripetal force required ∝ radius^-1.00; factor = 5.00^-1.00 = 0.200. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Show that the expressions a = v²/r and a = rω² are equivalent. (b) Explain why a car is more likely to skid outwards on a bend when it is travelling fast.
items.answer: (a) v = ωr, so v²/r = ω²r²/r = rω². (b) The centripetal force needed, mv²/r, increases with v²; friction has a maximum value, so above a certain speed friction cannot supply enough force and the car moves to a larger radius.
items.markingKey: (a) substitute v = ωr [1]; simplify to rω² [1] [2] (b) required force ∝ v² [1]; friction limited, so insufficient [1] [2]

items.stem: A runner of mass 78 kg moves round a bend of radius 36.5 m at a constant speed of 8.0 m s⁻¹. Work out the centripetal force.
items.markingKey: F = mv²/r = 78 × 8.0²/36.5 = 137 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A astronaut-training centrifuge of radius 9.0 m rotates at 20 revolutions per minute. Calculate the centripetal acceleration at the rim and express it as a multiple of g.

An aircraft of mass 50 000 kg moves round a horizontal circle of radius 2000 m at a constant speed of 240 m s⁻¹. Calculate the angular speed and the centripetal force, and state what provides this force.
items.answer: ω = 0.12 rad s⁻¹; F = 1.44 × 10⁶ N; provided by the horizontal component of the lift force
items.markingKey: ω = v/r = 0.12 rad s⁻¹ [1]; F = mv²/r = 1.44 × 10⁶ N [1]; the horizontal component of the lift force [1] [3]

items.stem: A ball of mass 0.20 kg on a string moves at constant speed 3.0 m s⁻¹ round a horizontal circle of radius 0.75 m on a smooth table. (a) Calculate the angular speed. (b) Calculate the centripetal force. (c) State what provides the centripetal force.
items.answer: (a) 4.0 rad s⁻¹ (b) 2.40 N (c) The tension in the string.
items.markingKey: (a) ω = v/r: 4.0 rad s⁻¹ [1] (b) F = mv²/r (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.40 N with unit [1] [2] (c) The tension in the string [1]

items.stem: A train of mass 2.00 × 10⁵ kg moves at constant speed 30 m s⁻¹ round a curve of radius 900 m. (a) Explain why a resultant force is needed even though the speed is constant. (b) Calculate the angular speed. (c) Calculate the centripetal acceleration.
items.answer: (a) The direction of the velocity changes, so there is an acceleration (towards the centre), which requires a resultant force (F = ma). (b) 0.0333 rad s⁻¹ (c) 1.0 m s⁻²
items.markingKey: (a) velocity changes [1]; resultant force towards centre [1] [2] (b) ω = v/r: 0.0333 rad s⁻¹ [1] (c) a = v²/r (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.0 m s⁻² with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In a conical pendulum, what provides the centripetal force on the bob? (b) State the condition for an object on a string to just complete a vertical circle.
items.answer: (a) the horizontal component of the tension (b) At the top, the tension is zero and the weight alone provides the centripetal force (mg = mv²/r).
items.markingKey: (a) T sin θ = mv²/r; T cos θ balances the weight. (b) T = 0 at top, mg = mv²/r [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the reading on a scale under a passenger in a big wheel is smaller at the top of the ride than at the bottom. (b) Explain why water stays in a bucket swung quickly in a vertical circle, even when the bucket is upside down at the top.
items.answer: (a) At the top, mg − N = mv²/r, so N = mg − mv²/r < mg; at the bottom, N − mg = mv²/r, so N = mg + mv²/r > mg. (b) At the top, the centripetal force needed (mv²/r) is greater than the weight of the water, so the bucket base must push down on the water; the water stays pressed against the base. If v were too small, mg > mv²/r and the water would fall out.
items.markingKey: (a) top: N = mg − mv²/r [1]; bottom: N = mg + mv²/r [1] [2] (b) required centripetal force > weight [1]; base pushes on water / water stays in contact [1] [2]

items.stem: A conical pendulum consists of a bob of mass 0.20 kg on a string of length 0.80 m. The bob moves in a horizontal circle with the string at 50° to the vertical. Calculate the tension in the string and the radius of the circle.

A test track in Dubai has a bend of radius 250 m. It is banked so that a vehicle travelling at 30 m s⁻¹ needs no sideways friction. By resolving the normal contact force, show that tan θ = v²/(rg) and calculate the angle of banking.
items.answer: N cos θ = mg, N sin θ = mv²/r ⇒ tan θ = v²/(rg); θ = 20.2°
items.markingKey: N cos θ = mg [1]; N sin θ = mv²/r and divide [1]; θ = 20.2° [1] [3]
